source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 25% of people in Czechia were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
15.5% of health spending in Czechia was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
0.5% of people in Czechia reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
5% of hospital care costs in Czechia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
8% of outpatient medical care costs in Czechia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
56% of dental care costs in Czechia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
43% of pharmaceutical costs in Czechia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

However, over 8% of the population reported unmet care needs in Latvia (8.4%), Estonia (8.5%), Finland (8.6%), Canada (9.1%) and Greece (12.1%), while in Germany, the Netherlands and Czechia, fewer than 1% of the population reported unmet needs for medical care.

There are also some variations in the survey questions across countries: while most countries refer to both a medical examination and treatment, the question in some countries (Czechia and Spain) only refers to a medical examination or a doctor consultation, resulting in lower rates of unmet needs.
In contrast, government and compulsory insurance schemes paid over 90% of these costs in Czechia, the Slovak Republic, Sweden, Germany, Denmark and the United Kingdom.
For example, in Czechia, almost all health services are free at the point of use, except for a small fee for out-of-hours outpatient care.
Disparities were smallest in Czechia, France and Japan, where more than 98% of people in rural areas had access to hospitals nearby.
Iceland, Portugal, Italy, Korea and Sweden reported rates lower than 12 per 100 000 population, while Chile, Czechia, Slovenia and Germany reported rates higher than 40 per 100 000.
Rates ranged from over 50% in Greece and Saudi Arabia, to under 10% in Czechia and Switzerland (Figure 6.20).
